messages:
eva_h: Heads-up — after deploying the batcher tweak last night, we see a 95th-tail latency regression on short completions when prefix cache hit rate is high (>70%). Spike happens ~token 4-8 and stacks when there's a mix of cache-hit and miss requests in the same batch.

samuel: ugh, saw a similar blip in staging but chalked it up to a noisy GPU run. do you have traces/prof?

eva_h: pasted a minimal flame output below (sensitive lines redacted). note the kernel fallback during the mixed batch.

jordan-r: perf-bot posted the alert too:
perf-bot: regression alert: model-ggml-v2 serving v2026-03-16 -> +18% p95 latency on short prompts (canary). Tags: kv_cache_hit:mixed, batch_size:variable, kernel_fallback:true

li: can you share the batch composition stats? size distribution, %cache-hit per batch? that matters for the packing heuristic.

eva_h: quick stats from the 2h window: avg batch size 6, 40% batches are mixed (>=1 hit && >=1 miss), mixed batches p95 = 420ms, homogeneous-hit batches p95 = 120ms, homogeneous-miss p95 = 160ms.

samuel: interesting — homogeneous-hit much faster, mixed worst. suggests packing should avoid mixing hits+misses for short-tokens. current packer favors fill-to-budget.

liam: kernel selection may be flipping on mixed KV cache since cached requests have shorter seq len after prefix chop -> runtime switches to small-seq kernels but still has to run miss paths for other requests, causing scheduling overhead.

jordan-r: agree. we also saw token budget logic tries to pack to target tokens_per_batch (TPB) and doesn't account for KV cache hit reducing future token work. result: batch becomes heterogeneous and causes inefficient kernel pathing.

eva_h: proposed quick fix: add a cache-hit-aware soft partition in the queueing layer. if head-of-queue is hit-dominant, group next N only with hit-dominant requests up to token budget, else form miss group.

samuel: sketch of heuristic I tried locally:
```
# simple pseudo
if head.cache_hit_ratio >= 0.75:
  allow_mixed = False
  target_tokens = min(global_token_budget, head.estimated_tokens)
else:
  allow_mixed = True
  target_tokens = global_token_budget
# then pack requests respecting allow_mixed flag
```

li: nice. also add metric tags like batch.kv_hit_ratio and batch.kernel_variant so we can alert on mixed batches causing kernel_fallback.

jordan-r: can we avoid hard partitioning? maybe use priority queue with two lanes (hit / miss) and a short merge window: try to flush same-lane first for X ms or until token budget near limit, then merge. keeps throughput but reduces harmful mixing.

eva_h: that seems promising — setting merge window to 3ms removed 75% of mixed-batch regressions in my local sim.

liam: watch out for fairness. for very sparse hit or miss lanes, we might starve the other lane. add eviction-based aging or an absolute max-wait-per-request.

samuel: experiment plan: A/B in canary with two configs
- config A: soft partition (allow_mixed flag)
- config B: two-lane PQ with merge window 3ms + max_wait 50ms
Collect: p50/p95/p99, batch.kv_hit_ratio histogram, kernel_variant counts, throughput, and user-level tail errors.

perf-bot: scheduled job: run canary A on 10% traffic and canary B on 10% traffic starting in 30m.

li: also add a lightweight instrument: per-request KV cache prediction (bool) at enqueue time so batches can be analyzed offline. don't rely on expensive traces.

eva_h: will add metric and push a small patch to packer. i'll post the branch and flame samples. thanks all :thumbsup:

jordan-r: one more note — check quantization kernel selection heuristics too. mixed batches sometimes trigger fallback to FP kernels in our runtime when memory access patterns get weird. might need a small change in kernel_chooser to prefer stable path if mixed batch detected.

liam: noted. I'll run microbench with mixed vs homogeneous kernels tomorrow.

samuel: great thread. let's reconvene after the canary runs. if A or B fixes p95 we can include a configurable default in next minor release.

perf-bot: canary started at 1796341200 (A:10%, B:10%).
